Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
abstract: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. title: Hamed Karimi wins ECML PKDD Test-of-Time Award
abstract: In Naples last month, at the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML PKDD), Amazon senior applied scientist Hamed Karimi and colleagues won the 2026 ECML PKDD Test-of-Time Award for their 2016 paper “Linear convergence of gradient and proximal-gradient methods under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition”. The award recognizes research published a decade earlier that has had a lasting impact. The paper, written with Julie Nutini and Mark Schmidt while Karimi was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of British Columbia, has helped to organize a previously scattered field of machine learning optimization and offers useful approaches to analyzing new training methods. “When we wrote the paper in 2016, we genuinely didn’t expect it to make a splash,” Karimi says. “We did not know that the result would become part of the way researchers analyze optimization in machine learning.” Karimi and his coauthors showed that the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition, a 1963 mathematical inequality that had been largely overlooked in machine learning, can prove that the standard method for training machine learning models closes in on the best solutions quickly, even when many different solutions could work equally well. Because modern machine learning models rarely have a single best solution, the result helped close a long-standing gap between what training methods do in practice and what theory could guarantee. Optimization landscape In the classic supervised-machine-learning setting, a model’s billions of settings, or parameters, are adjusted so that the model’s outputs match labeled training data as closely as possible. The distance between the model’s output and the labeled data is measured with a loss function; the goal is to tune the parameters to minimize the loss. This tuning is done through optimization processes, the most common approach being gradient descent or one of its variants. One way to understand gradient descent is to visualize a topographic map with peaks, valleys, cliffs, and plateaus. The lowest points on the map represent minimal loss, with each step downhill toward these minima representing parameter adjustments that optimize toward fewer errors. Ideally, researchers would like to know the quickest path to the bottom. Theory suggests that the fastest path shrinks the error by a constant fraction each step, a property known as linear convergence. The problem is that linear convergence is mathematically guaranteed only for a particular topographic shape: a steep bowl that uniformly curves upward, one that is strongly convex. A bowl like this has exactly one lowest point, so from any location, there is a single best move toward optimization. But many real problems don't work that way. When training data are redundant, as is the case with modern large language models, where the parameter count is disproportionately large compared to the amount of training data, the bottom of the landscape becomes a flat valley floor instead of a single point at the bottom of a bowl. These models — which exhibit weaker conditions than convexity — can be successfully trained with gradient descent, but the theory could neither explain why nor say how quickly, leaving a gap between what works in practice and what can be proven. By 2016, some 25 years’ worth of solutions to optimization problems with weaker conditions were in circulation, each with its own name, notation, and paper, but nobody had established how they related. Karimi and his colleagues’ paper settled those relationships. Researchers have since used variations of the paper’s method to rederive guarantees for essentially every standard optimization algorithm in machine learning. The paper has been cited over 2,000 times and has found a place in graduate textbooks. title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
abstract: When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator. This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An ml.p4d.24xlarge has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach. Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation. This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did. One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components , the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned. What customers do today, and why each option falls short If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices. Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not. Use multi-model endpoints – These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic. But models share the device without isolation, so a heavy request for one model affects the others. A model that isn’t loaded also pays a load penalty on first use. Move to self-managed Kubernetes – This is where customers who need real GPU partitioning have gone. MIG works there, but you take on driver versioning, partition configuration, a device plugin, scheduling, and keeping it all consistent across a fleet. That’s a lot of work for a hardware capability your instances already have. Why MIG NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give: Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99. Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU. Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device. No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction. Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler. title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick
abstract: Over the past year, as we built Amazon Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user. Take the user who says “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice. This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When? , What? , Who? , and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it. The framework at a glance Figure 1: How triggers, agents, and capabilities relate, with learning feeding back from the session runtime A trigger starts the work and carries the task ( When and What ), an agent takes it on ( Who ) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task ( How ). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more. Triggers: What causes work to begin Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task. Human-initiated: A person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something. Interactive, synchronous, conversational. Agent-delegated: One agent, mid-task, invokes another to handle a sub-problem. Programmatic, composable, potentially recursive. Scheduled: Time-based activation, like “run financial research every Monday at 9am.” Deterministic, with the same standing instructions applied across runs. Event-driven: A signal from an external system, such as a new email, a Slack mention, a file change, or a webhook. The type of trigger conditions the execution: a scheduled background task might stay conservative (for example, do nothing if uncertain), while a human-initiated one would be responsive (for example, ask rather than stop). Agents We define an agent as a persistent, learning actor . It’s the Who? in any execution, and the anchor against which learning accrues. Two agents given identical input can differ, because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories. The agent isn’t the instructions it follows. It’s the entity that interprets them. It consists of three things: Instructions: Standing guidance defining persona, role, context files, and operating principles. A Finance Agent behaves differently from a general assistant primarily because of this. Capabilities: The tools, skills, workflows, and sub-agents available for use, updated dynamically. A charting library can be added in one session and removed the next. Learned context: Memory that accumulates through use: the queries that work for a tool, the formatting users prefer, the edge cases they care about. This is how the tenth execution beats the first without anyone changing the instructions. Everything else is extrinsic: the large language model (LLM) underlying the agent is a swappable model parameter, conversation history is per-session state, and triggers belong to the platform. title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
abstract: Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort. Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync. In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment. Problem statement and design goals Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model. Integration challenge at scale Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table. Design goals We established four requirements: Configuration-driven data lake access. Adding a dataset requires only a metadata file, not code. Agent-agnostic tool interfaces. Any MCP-compatible client can invoke the same tools. Centralized permission enforcement. Access control is enforced at the MCP server layer. Elastic infrastructure. The system scales with bursty AI workload patterns. Solution overview The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge-base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable. A metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, storing schema descriptions, column-level semantics, and table relationships that the AI agent references when generating SQL. Because the agent derives schema knowledge from the catalog at query time, there is no need to hardcode table structures or redeploy when schemas change. The knowledge-base refresh layer keeps that catalog current, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives. The following sections describe each layer in detail. Architecture walkthrough The following diagram shows the request flow from user query to data layer across all four layers. A user submits a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53 for DNS and reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet, configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer routes to Amazon Cognito, which authenticates the user and enriches the request. Authenticated traffic then enters the private subnet, where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate. This layer handles session state in Amazo

title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
abstract: In Part 1 , you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server. The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant. The BFF invokes agent A on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG. Agent A forwards the ID-JAG to its Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer accepts only agent A’s ID-JAGs. Policy in AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies for each tool listing and each tool call, before the Gateway invokes a target. Every hop emits OpenTelemetry spans to AgentCore Observability, which CloudWatch Transaction Search collects, and Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge. title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
abstract: An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end. In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. Solution overview Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime. Figure 1: Solution architecture, with numbers matching the steps that follow Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this: The user signs in to the web front end, a backend for frontend (BFF), with OpenID Connect through the agent’s linked Okta app. For each request, the BFF exchanges the user’s ID token for an ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server, authenticated as the agent (RFC 8693 token exchange). Okta checks that the agent is active, that the user is assigned to it, and that an administrator connected it to the target authorization server for the requested scopes. The ID-JAG is single-use and expires in 5 minutes. The BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG as its bearer token. title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Greenlight Financial resolves more than 90 percent of up to 4,000 security and risk cases each month without human intervention. Greenlight’s Luna uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , infrastructure for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale. Specifically, Greenlight uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to host Luna’s agent code. It uses AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to support its tiered multi-agent system. This avoids the need to build and operate these capabilities in-house. Luna triages dark web breach-card alerts, identity anomalies, and financial-risk events in seconds. This post explains how Greenlight Financial built an autonomous security operations center (SOC) solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover its multi-tiered supervisor architecture, more than 30 specialized agents, episodic memory for continuous learning, and expansion from SOC use cases into financial risk triage. We share production metrics, infrastructure decisions, and patterns for building autonomous security operations in regulated industries. What Greenlight needed to solve Greenlight Financial provides financial products for families: debit cards, savings tools, and connected devices such as the Family Hub and Pet Tracker. The company processes sensitive financial data at scale under the same regulatory requirements as major banks. Greenlight’s SOC receives 3,000–4,000 security and risk alerts per month from four primary vectors: Dark web breach cards – Card Network and internal threat intel flag Greenlight customer cards found on the dark web. Identity and access anomalies – Unusual login patterns, privilege escalations, and policy violations across Identity Provider (IdP) and internal systems. Infrastructure alerts – Signals from Signals from EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), Asset Inventory, and other observability tools. Financial risk events – Suspicious transaction patterns, compliance triggers, and fraud indicators from card processing systems. Each alert demands cross-referencing multiple data sources before an analyst can render a verdict. A single dark web breach card notification requires checking whether the card is active, deduplicating against prior notifications, reviewing customer session data, and checking open support tickets. This workflow takes a human analyst 15-30 minutes per case. At 4,000 cases per month, that math breaks. Greenlight needed a system that could: Triage and resolve routine cases autonomously at machine speed. Escalate complex cases with full context to human analysts. Learn from resolution patterns to improve accuracy over time. Operate within financial services compliance guardrails. title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Taxbit is a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform. Founded in 2018, Taxbit helps enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers calculate gains and losses, collect tax documentation, and file information returns at scale. Now, a cited, permission-aware AI assistant helps compliance teams find answers right inside the product dashboard. But the knowledge needed to use that dashboard well was scattered across the public website, API documentation, and help-center articles, and a meaningful share was never written down at all. When a customer asked “what does this form status mean?”, they either went digging or filed a support ticket. Today more than 55 percent of users who ask Assist a question return to ask another within 24 hours, according to Taxbit’s internal production analytics. In this post, we share how we built Taxbit Assist , the AI assistant now embedded in the Taxbit dashboard, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. We cover the architecture, the retrieval work that made answers trustworthy enough to ship to regulated customers, how we handle safety and data residency, and how we continuously measure answer quality on live production traffic. What the assistant had to get right A generic chatbot was not an option in this domain. Four constraints shaped what we built: Grounded and cited – Our users make filing decisions. Every answer had to trace back to a source the user could open and read, and when the assistant didn’t know something, it had to say so. Role and organization awareness – The assistant shouldn’t walk a Support User through an admin-only workflow and send them to a page that they can’t open. No tax advice – Explaining how Taxbit computes cost basis (the accounting method used to compute a gain or loss) is product documentation. Telling a user which method to elect is tax advice. The line between the two is narrow. Regional data residency – Supported from a single codebase, with continuous quality measurement in production. Inside our compliance program – Taxbit Assist is developed and operated in line with ISO/IEC 42001, the international standard for AI management systems. Taxbit is also certified to ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27701 and holds a SOC 2 Type II report. Taxbit doesn’t train or fine-tune any model, and Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use prompts or completions to train models. We are also a small team. Rather than build and operate the agent loop, conversation-state store, and session isolation ourselves, we chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for three reasons: its managed agent runtime removed infrastructure operations, built-in AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, eliminated a separate conversation-state store, and per-session isolation kept each user’s context contained. That let us put most of our effort into the retrieval and safety work that follows. abstract: You might already run Claude Code locally on your laptop, backed by Amazon Bedrock. The sample uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so every task runs in its own isolated session inside your AWS account. title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves. If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart. The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent. What Web Answer does Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result. Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back: A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available. Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information. Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer. Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards. Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer How it differs from Web Search Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model: Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed. Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it. Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. abstract: A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content. A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count. Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality. With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners. To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals. In this post, you will learn how to: Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM. Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations. Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners. Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT) , splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space ( Flamingo , LLaVA ). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP , which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale. title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
abstract: Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model. Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong. This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev , a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B , an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an AgentCore evaluation result. First, though, when should you reach for a custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, and when does a decision model fit better? The next section breaks down what a decision model is and the trade-offs involved. Decision models A decision model is a small, specialized model trained to select from a fixed set of options and return calibrated confidence scores rather than generating free-form text. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) evaluator produces a score with a rationale. A decision model instead produces a probability distribution over predefined answers. That gives you a direct confidence measure you can threshold, aggregate, and act on programmatically. This makes decision models well-suited for evaluation tasks where the judgment can be stated as a choice among a fixed set of options: “Is this response grounded?” or “Did the agent complete the user’s goal?” Decision models are most useful when you want a well-calibrated confidence score alongside the label, not just a binary judgment. They are also appropriate when you want to enforce a specific rubric consistently without relying on a general-purpose LLM to interpret it. Jev, the hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider , an open-source, 2-billion-parameter decision model from the Strands Agents team, both support three types of questions. A noul question poses a yes/no question and returns a probability between 0 (no) and 1 (yes). title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
abstract: How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts , even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review. Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work. Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked Policy sets the boundary Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions. Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them. How eligible actions are reviewed Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service. An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions. The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
abstract: When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent. This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight , an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout. Post series Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them. Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!) The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK , Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations. What is context engineering? Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “ Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report ” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes. Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing. “As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).” — Anthropic, “ Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents ” (2025.09) Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
abstract: This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited. Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise. This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs. About Indegene Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments. Why conventional data quality programs break down Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve. One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult. Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent. Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly. Additionally, the operational impact is significant. title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it. The problem: Too many systems, too much friction U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud. Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration. The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars. Reach : agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time. Depth : chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis. Community : a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division. This Week in AI: The Cost of Progress
abstract: New frontier models arrived this week as investors showed signs of growing cautious about AI spending. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined those developments, along with research into how models learn and the less visible costs of AI adoption. From unequal pricing across languages to the environmental impact of data centers, the discussion raised questions about who benefits from AI progress and who pays for it. Frontier models advance as investors question the spending We started with three model announcements that show how quickly AI capabilities are expanding. Google introduced Gemini 4 Carbon , designed for cybersecurity and complex, multistep tasks. France’s Mistral published the weights for its trillion-parameter Large 4 model , also known as “Le Chonk,” giving developers more control over deployment and customization, provided they have the hardware to run it. Meanwhile, Google DeepMind previewed Genie 4 , a world model that simulates environments, physical interactions, and sequences of events. Unlike language models that predict text, world models attempt to predict what happens when objects and people interact. With Genie 4, researchers could train AI systems in simulated worlds, an approach that would be especially useful in robotics, where teams could test AI designed to control robots before trying it on physical machines. Investor enthusiasm for AI appeared to weaken even as model development accelerated. Anthropic moved closer to a public offering by filing its IPO paperwork publicly , although it hasn’t announced a date or share price. OpenAI has reportedly secured about $11 billion in funding for its latest round, well below its initial $30 billion target. Those developments coincided with sharp declines in several major technology stocks , and the tech-heavy Nasdaq ended October with its worst monthly decline since March 2025. The scale of AI spending is attracting greater scrutiny, particularly as investors wait for returns. Companies investing in AI should pay attention to more than model performance. The economics of training and running increasingly expensive models could affect pricing, availability, and which providers remain competitive. Researchers are rethinking how AI models learn Researchers are investigating how AI models process information, retain knowledge, and generate responses. AI interpretability company Goodfire proposed a project modeled on the Human Genome Project , committing $10 million to begin mapping how large language models work internally. By studying which patterns activate in response to prompts and how changes to those patterns affect behavior, researchers hope to better understand why models produce particular outputs. Google Research proposed a framework inspired by human cognition that introduces a “sleep” phase. During this offline period, models would consolidate new information and generate practice examples through a process researchers call “dreaming.” The goal is to address catastrophic forgetting, when learning new information degrades previously acquired capabilities, while helping models retain knowledge beyond individual conversations. The approach remains experimental, but it offers a possible way for models to continue learning without sacrificing existing skills. We also examined Clover, a 35-billion-parameter diffusion language model released by China’s DiffuSpace. Most familiar language models use what’s called an autoregressive approach: They generate text sequentially, one token at a time. Diffusion language models instead work on multiple parts of an answer simultaneously, refining them over successive passes. DiffuSpace reports competitive performance and faster generation on some tasks when compared to autoregressive models of similar size. title: Choose Your Coding Harness by What You Need to Control—Not by Who Built It
abstract: Remember back in 2019, when you had only a handful of language models to choose from, all with limited context windows? That world is gone, and it feels like a forgotten past. Today, flagship providers and open source projects compete across model families, sizes, capabilities, and deployment options. Coding harnesses seem to be heading in the same direction. On the surface, Claude Code, Codex, Pi, DeepSeek Harness, and the other coding harnesses all seem to do the same thing: help you build software with models. Look closer, though, and each one gives you control over different parts of the harness. What can the model see and change? How does it use tools? Where does it run, and what happens when it fails? So instead of asking which coding harness is best overall, ask: Which layers of the harness do you need to control? Thanks for all the harnesses! Now what? Choosing a coding harness isn’t only about which model writes the best code. You’re also choosing what the harness provides, what you can change, and what you must build yourself. If it doesn’t give you verification, durable state, repair routing, or an enforced execution boundary, those responsibilities stay with you. You remain accountable for the workflow’s reliability and governance. In general, each harness has a center of gravity: a layer that gives you the most direct control. The following table is a deliberately high-level overview of where that center sits. It’s not a feature matrix, and the boundaries overlap in practice. Claude Code can also run noninteractively and inside sandboxes, Codex also reads repository instructions, and all of them are changing quickly. The point is to show where each harness gives you leverage by default, and where the engineering work is likely to stay with you. Table 1. Where each coding harness puts its primary control Harness Primary control You shape You likely build Claude Code Inside the run Instructions, skills, subagents, hooks Outer lifecycle policy Codex Around execution Sandbox, approvals, scope, output Cross-run orchestration Pi The loop itself Tools, context, state, hand-offs Most defaults DeepSeek Across plug-ins Composable runtime components Gaps in your plug-in set Read the table as a map, not a ranking. A harness that hands you more control also hands you more to build, and a harness that does more out of the box decides more on your behalf. Which trade-off is right depends on which layer your project actually needs to own. Claude Code: Control inside the run Claude Code buys you detailed control over how implementation unfolds. CLAUDE.md provides standing instructions, skills add task-specific playbooks, subagents divide the work, and hooks intercept actions before and after tool calls. Unlike a permission rule that simply refuses an operation, a hook can explain the refusal or immediately return a compiler or policy failure to the agent. These controls let you steer the coding loop extensively, but they operate within Claude Code’s existing lifecycle. If you need to control the outer lifecycle itself, you need another layer. Codex: Control through separation Codex buys you separation between a coding task and its execution environment. A noninteractive codex exec run can work on a narrow task in a specified repository, under an OS-enforced sandbox, and return a schema-constrained result. This is useful for independent verification. You can give Codex a clean checkout, exclude the builder’s instructions, restrict writable paths, and run separate reviews for code quality, test gaps, persistence, or user-visible behavior. The sandbox depends on the operating system, but it moves scope enforcement out of the prompt and into the execution boundary. title: The New Knowledge Artifacts of the AI Economy
abstract: At our recent Foo Camp , a number of people said something like, “I don’t want someone else’s code any more. I may have my agent take a look at it, but I want to extract just the parts that I want, and may rewrite even those in Rust. It’s just too easy to create just the code that I want.” This topic was hot enough that Jesse Vincent held an entire session about it. I did not attend, but Jesse gave me a report from his Plaude AI notetaker. Here’s a relevant section of the summary: Several participants argue that software development’s primary artifact may be shifting from executable code toward natural-language prompts, generation processes, and developer skills. One speaker compares Python to assembly language, suggesting that writing conventional code may become optional as natural-language generation takes precedence. Another argues that open source can survive such a transition because its core values—peer production, capacity building, and shared specifications—do not depend on who or what writes the code. At the same time, Jesse warns that maintainers are overwhelmed by floods of uninvited, automated, and often low-quality contributions. Participants say that traditional milestones such as pull requests, repositories, and conferences have helped contributors connect and gain recognition; as AI makes code replication easier, communities may need new ways to acknowledge participation and create paths for future developers. Some community interaction has moved to spaces such as Discord and direct messages, but structured opportunities are still needed. Scientific computing raises particular concerns. One panelist warns that AI-generated forks and agent attacks could threaten carefully verified foundations such as NumPy and SciPy. Scientific systems depend on battle-tested libraries and reproducibility, so thousands of unreviewed alternatives could undermine reliability. Participants suggest bridging traditional open-source communities and modern AI development, which currently may use different tools and artifacts. Other proposals include treating code as “liquid” and focusing open-source governance on durable infrastructure and specifications; maintaining agent storage independently of ephemeral container lifecycles; and using corporate compliance and safety-monitoring architectures to aggregate organizational traces. These are important observations, all pointing in the same direction: AI is transforming the mechanisms and the artifacts of software development. For an increasing number of use cases, the software source code itself may no longer be the most important shareable knowledge artifact. This isn’t a new phenomenon. Every major change in technology calls for new mechanisms, new artifacts, and new institutions. Originally, software developers mostly distributed binaries, then open source developers made sharing source code the norm. Now we need to distribute and share something else: context and patterns for generating code on the fly. Knowledge is being unbundled and can be shared in new forms. A repo may now serve merely as a source of context for solving the exact problem I have, rather than the bundle of problems that the original developer(s) encoded into their library or packaged solution. Some people will keep their context and patterns private, either because they see proprietary advantage in keeping them to themselves or because they are too busy or too lazy to share. But part of the problem is that we haven’t yet figured out what needs to be shared! The challenge for the software development community is to identify the new knowledge artifacts of the AI economy, and to build new mechanisms and incentives for sharing them. We’ve all had the experience of seeing a bespoke agentically generated app, wanting something similar, and wishing we could ask for a starting point so we didn’t have to vibe code an equivalent from scratch, with all the attention, false starts, and token costs that comes with that. title: What It Takes To Trust Automatic Model Routing
abstract: When a new coding model comes out, I want to try it. New releases always carry a promise for me. Maybe it can handle a change that needed too much manual intervention before. Maybe it can find the problem an earlier model kept missing. Maybe it can handle some coding scenarios that my favorite model can’t handle today. To discover a new model’s capabilities, I need to spend time with it to find out what I can reasonably hand over to it. Having said all that, I understand the frustration when a new model becomes available, but your assistant won’t let you choose that model. Somebody has decided which models you can use and when you can use them. You are left trying to decide whether the answer is good enough and can’t get your hands on the new shiny toys. At the same time, I’m quite happy to let an assistant choose a model if that makes my budget last longer. New toys tend to be expensive and top-line models don’t make a difference here. There are plenty of steps in development where a cheaper model might do everything required. Using it for those steps could leave more of the budget available for a difficult investigation later. If routing lets me keep using capable assistance throughout the day, I have a good reason to use it. I want routing to give me more assistance for the same budget. The quality of that assistance depends on how the models, tools, and context handling fit together. And I need enough information about what the assistant did to judge the result. Getting more help from the same budget A fixed AI budget puts a fairly ordinary constraint on a team. Or better, on the affected individual. You have an amount you can spend, and of course you want as much help as possible from it. Each request uses some of that amount. And it really gets frustrating when repeating a request, correcting an answer, and asking the assistant to try again consume even more of the budget. Automatic routing gives the system a way to manage that spending for you. It can use a cheaper model where that model is likely to succeed and spend more where the additional capability is likely to help. You, the developer, can then concentrate on the task while the assistant handles some of these decisions and you don’t have to constantly worry about which model to pick for which task. The researchers behind RouteLLM trained routers to choose between a stronger model and a cheaper one using preference data. They reported more than a twofold reduction in cost with minimal impact on response quality on the benchmarks they evaluated. You still need to check how it performs on your own tasks. The next question is how those savings get to me in my day-to-day jobs. If requests become cheaper to serve, the same subscription could support more of them. A team could keep its assistant available to more people within an existing spending limit. The saving could also make it practical to use a more capable model more often when the task calls for it. So much for the theory. In most assistants that behavior is little more than a “switch.” That connection to better results needs to be visible in the product. If I choose automatic routing, I want to understand what I get from it. Perhaps I can send more requests before I reach a limit. The results still need to meet my expectations, of course. This is a fairly reasonable thing to ask of a feature that spends part of the budget on my behalf. The time we spend with the assistant belongs in that calculation too. Think about how a cheaper request can lead to another attempt, followed by another explanation, followed by a correction. If this happens often enough, I spend more time getting the code ready to accept than I would have with a more capable model. So when we compare routing policies, we need to follow the task through those interactions. Then we can look at both the money spent and the time we put into getting there and compare both together. title: Resonant Computing and Common Fabric
abstract: This event summary was created by Claude with editing by Tim O’Reilly, based on a transcript of the conversation. Alex Komoroske is the CEO and a cofounder of Common Fabric , a public benefit corporation building the infrastructure for human-centric agentic computing. He spent more than a decade at Google as a product manager and director of product management on Chrome, Google Maps, and Google Earth, and he later ran corporate strategy at Stripe. At O’Reilly’s AI Codecon a year earlier, in a talk called “ Why Centralized AI Is Not Our Inevitable Future ,” he argued that we were sleepwalking into the wrong future for AI and didn’t have to accept it. Since then he has coauthored the Resonant Computing Manifesto , which Tim signed. On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Tim O’Reilly hosted Alex for an hour-long conversation, “ Can We Build More-Human Technology? ” Common Fabric’s consumer product hasn’t yet been released, but Alex showed Tim the product privately the day before, and Tim said his conversations with Alex had left him “more optimistic about the future of the web and the AI future than I’ve been in a long time.” They talked about the underlying theory behind Common Fabric. The Resonant Computing Manifesto The Resonant Computing Manifesto lays out five principles for resonant technology. It is private , meaning you’re the steward of your own data and it’s used in accordance with your wishes. It is dedicated , with no conflicts of interest. It is plural , with no central entity holding an unnecessary amount of power. It is adaptable , able to do things its creators didn’t specifically build in. And it is prosocial , helping people create meaning together rather than living as “individual islands.” According to Alex, the manifesto rests on a distinction between two kinds of experience. A hollow thing is something that you like when you’re using it, and then, after you’re done using it, you’re left feeling regret. And a resonant thing is something that you like when you’re using it, and then afterwards you’re left feeling nourished. They are superficially very similar, but they’re fundamentally, deeply, structurally different. Alex argued that modern tech, business, and politics are very good at delivering hollow experiences efficiently and poor at delivering resonant ones. The manifesto came from a group of people who still believe in the hacker ethic of the 1990s and early 2000s, he said. They believe that technology is a large positive force for humanity, but also that the industry has spent the last decade optimizing for engagement and extraction, which has undermined that positive impact. They think that the AI transition is a unique opportunity to reset the norms and the architecture to make something that works better for people than for extractive business models. Privacy, bits, and the physics of trust Tim started out by asking Alex to go a bit deeper on privacy. Privacy and trust are related in ways the privacy movement often doesn’t consider, Tim said. We don’t put bars on all of our windows. We trust most people not to break in because we built a society where trust is the norm. It’s held in place not just by penalties but by social rewards for people who follow norms. “People will think you’re a creep if you go look into somebody’s window,” Tim noted. Like bars on the window, hard privacy seems to Tim a bit like an admission that we’re giving up on positive social norms and penalties for rulebreakers (where needed). He wanted to know whether Alex meant “private” in the way that HIPAA makes your healthcare records private, where your data is made hard for anyone to see, including you. Alex doesn’t mean that at all. He means privacy that makes your data more useful by putting it under your control. He gave a three-part answer about how that happens.
